ne-a9f875c2.stem: Which tract carries fine touch and proprioception from the lower limb?
ne-a9f875c2.explanation: In the dorsal columns the medially placed fasciculus gracilis carries information from the lower trunk and leg, the laterally placed fasciculus cuneatus (above T6) from the upper trunk and arm. The fibres ascend on the same side, synapse in the medulla (gracile/cuneate nuclei) and cross to form the medial lemniscus.

ne-dda468ea.stem: A patient who burns their hands on a hot stove without noticing has a 'cape-like' loss of pain and temperature over both shoulders and arms; touch and position sense are preserved. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Subacute combined degeneration from B12 deficiency
ne-dda468ea.explanation: In syringomyelia the central canal widens and first damages the spinothalamic fibres crossing in the anterior white commissure, so pain and temperature are lost on both sides in a 'cape' over the affected segments. The dorsal columns are spared (dissociated sensory loss).

ne-4634c777.stem: Which of the following is usually preserved in anterior spinal artery occlusion?
options: Lower motor neuron function at the level of the lesion
ne-4634c777.explanation: The anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two thirds of the cord: the anterior horns and the corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts are affected. Because the dorsal columns are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, vibration and proprioception are preserved.

ne-bcf0f483.stem: Which tracts are affected in subacute combined degeneration due to vitamin B12 deficiency?
options: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts
Only the motor neurons of the anterior horn
Anterior white commissure and lateral horns
ne-bcf0f483.explanation: B12 deficiency impairs myelin synthesis and affects in particular the dorsal columns (loss of deep sensation, ataxia) together with the lateral corticospinal tracts (spasticity, Babinski sign).

ne-f37384b3.stem: A young man struck on the head with a baseball bat briefly loses consciousness and recovers, then deteriorates hours later. CT shows a biconvex (lens-shaped) haemorrhage that does not cross the sutures. In which space is the bleed and what is its source?
ne-f37384b3.explanation: An epidural haematoma forms between the skull and the dura, usually from arterial bleeding; because the dura is firmly attached at the sutures, the bleed does not cross them and is lens-shaped. A subdural haematoma comes from torn bridging veins, is crescent-shaped, crosses sutures and is common in the elderly and in alcoholics.

ne-56835093.stem: A patient presents with the worst headache of their life; the CSF is bloody and xanthochromic. What is the most common cause?
options: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery
Rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm of the cerebral arterial circle
ne-56835093.explanation: The commonest cause of non-traumatic subarachnoid haemorrhage is an aneurysm around the circle of Willis, most often at the anterior communicating artery junction. The blood mixes with the CSF in the subarachnoid space.

ne-c9d1565d.stem: Which tooth-like extensions of the pia mater attach the spinal cord to the dura mater on each side?
ne-c9d1565d.explanation: On each side the pia mater forms about 21 tooth-like extensions (denticulate ligaments) that pierce the arachnoid, attach to the dura and suspend the cord in the dural sac. The filum terminale runs from the conus medullaris to the coccyx.

ne-86030d28.stem: Which statement about the epidural space of the vertebral canal is correct?
options: It is freely continuous with an epidural space inside the skull.
It ends at L1 together with the spinal cord.
It lies between the pia mater and the arachnoid.
It contains fat and the internal vertebral venous plexus.
ne-86030d28.explanation: The spinal epidural space lies between the dura and the periosteum of the vertebral canal and contains fat and the valveless internal vertebral venous plexus (Batson). In the skull the dura is fused to the periosteum, so normally there is no epidural space; the space ends at the foramen magnum. These veins allow pelvic and breast cancers to spread to the spine.

ne-beeb8a52.stem: A patient with a massive lumbar disc herniation has 'saddle' anaesthesia over the perineum and inner thighs, urinary retention and reduced anal sphincter tone. What is this emergency?
options: Unilateral compression of the conus medullaris
ne-beeb8a52.explanation: When the nerve roots below L1–L2 (cauda equina) are compressed, the perineal skin, bladder and anal sphincter supplied by the sacral roots are affected. It requires urgent surgical decompression.

ne-80f02adb.stem: Which is the only sense that does not synapse in the thalamus before reaching the cortex?
ne-80f02adb.explanation: Olfactory fibres synapse in the olfactory bulb; the olfactory tract runs directly to areas such as the piriform cortex and the amygdala. All other senses are relayed in the thalamus before reaching the cortex.

ne-f7431de4.stem: A patient with headache and visual disturbance has lost the outer (temporal) visual fields of both eyes. A pituitary adenoma is suspected. Which structure is being compressed?
ne-f7431de4.explanation: In the optic chiasm the fibres from the nasal halves of both retinas cross; these fibres carry the temporal visual fields. A pituitary tumour pressing from below compresses them and causes bitemporal hemianopia.

ne-c94ccfe0.stem: Which visual field defect results from a lesion of the right optic tract?
options: Complete blindness of the right eye
ne-c94ccfe0.explanation: All lesions behind the chiasm cause a homonymous defect in the opposite visual field. The right optic tract carries fibres from the temporal retina of the right eye and the nasal retina of the left eye, that is, from the left visual field.

ne-cbc1f080.stem: Which defect is expected after damage to the optic radiation fibres passing through the temporal lobe (Meyer's loop)?
ne-cbc1f080.explanation: The lower fibres of the optic radiation (from the lower half of the retina, carrying the upper visual field) form Meyer's loop in the temporal lobe; their damage causes contralateral upper quadrantanopia ('pie in the sky'). Parietal lobe lesions affect the lower quadrant.

ne-48c33959.stem: A patient with a sudden, severe headache has ptosis, a fixed dilated pupil and a down-and-out deviation of the right eye. An aneurysm of which artery most often causes this picture?
ne-48c33959.explanation: The oculomotor nerve runs right beside the PCom. Because the parasympathetic pupillary fibres travel on the surface of the nerve, external compression (aneurysm) affects the pupil early. In diabetic (ischaemic) third nerve palsy the interior of the nerve is affected, so the pupil is usually spared.

ne-0abd7abf.stem: In which option are the three divisions of the trigeminal nerve correctly matched with the openings through which they leave the skull?
options: V1 – foramen rotundum, V2 – foramen ovale, V3 – foramen spinosum
V1 – superior orbital fissure, V2 – foramen rotundum, V3 – foramen ovale
V1 – foramen ovale, V2 – foramen rotundum, V3 – superior orbital fissure
V1 – optic canal, V2 – inferior orbital fissure, V3 – foramen ovale
V1 – superior orbital fissure, V2 – foramen ovale, V3 – foramen rotundum
ne-0abd7abf.explanation: The ophthalmic nerve passes through the superior orbital fissure into the orbit, the maxillary nerve through the foramen rotundum into the pterygopalatine fossa, and the mandibular nerve through the foramen ovale into the infratemporal fossa. Only V3 contains motor fibres.

ne-3ea7d066.stem: Which of the following muscles is NOT supplied by the mandibular nerve (V3)?
ne-3ea7d066.explanation: V3 supplies the muscles of the first pharyngeal arch: the muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid and the anterior belly of digastric. Stapedius is a second-arch muscle supplied by the facial nerve; its paralysis causes hyperacusis.

ne-119b3c5e.stem: Which nerves form the afferent and efferent limbs of the corneal reflex?
options: Afferent: ophthalmic nerve – Efferent: oculomotor nerve
Afferent: maxillary nerve (V2) – Efferent: oculomotor nerve
Afferent: optic nerve (II) – Efferent: oculomotor nerve (III)
Afferent: ophthalmic nerve (V1) – Efferent: facial nerve (VII)
Afferent: facial nerve – Efferent: trigeminal nerve
ne-119b3c5e.explanation: Touching the cornea is sensed by the nasociliary nerve (V1); in response orbicularis oculi (VII) contracts in both eyes. In the light reflex the afferent limb is II and the efferent III.

ne-2746f878.stem: A patient with facial palsy that began with pain behind the ear cannot wrinkle the forehead or close the eye on the same side, but taste, tear secretion and hearing are normal. Where is the lesion?
options: In the facial nucleus in the pons
At the level of the geniculate ganglion
Just before the chorda tympani leaves
At or distal to the stylomastoid foramen
ne-2746f878.explanation: In the facial canal the facial nerve gives off, in turn, the greater petrosal nerve (lacrimal gland), the nerve to stapedius and the chorda tympani (taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue). If only the muscles of facial expression are affected, the lesion lies after all these branches, at the stylomastoid foramen or in the parotid.

ne-f733b124.stem: Which option correctly lists the terminal branches into which the facial nerve divides within the parotid gland?
options: Temporal, infraorbital, buccal, mental and cervical branches
Ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular, buccal and cervical branches
Auricular, temporal, lingual, buccal and mental branches
Frontal, zygomatic, lingual, mandibular and cervical branches
Temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches
ne-f733b124.explanation: After leaving the stylomastoid foramen the facial nerve forms the pes anserinus within the parotid and divides into five terminal branches. Preserving these branches is the main priority in parotid surgery; the nerve does not supply the gland.

ne-fe75f44a.stem: A patient with progressive one-sided hearing loss and tinnitus has a reduced corneal reflex on the same side. MRI shows a mass at the cerebellopontine angle. What is the most likely diagnosis?
ne-fe75f44a.explanation: A vestibular schwannoma arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibular part of the vestibulocochlear nerve, grows in the internal acoustic meatus and extends into the cerebellopontine angle. As it grows it can compress the trigeminal nerve (corneal reflex) and the facial nerve.
